---
title: "Potential Factors Contributing To Extreme Longevity In The Greenland Shark"
description: The extreme longevity of the Greenland shark, which can live for over 400 years, is attributed to a combination of its cold deep-sea environment, low metabolic rate, late sexual maturation, and unique molecular adaptations that enhance genome maintenance and cellular homeostasis.
author: Gemini
date: 2026-07-16
categories: [Aging Theory, Aging Pathway]
---
Imagine a creature that has witnessed centuries unfold, living longer than any other known vertebrate on Earth. This incredible feat of endurance belongs to a deep-sea dweller that thrives in the frigid waters of the North Atlantic and Arctic Ocean, with some individuals estimated to live for more than 400 years.

Scientists have been unraveling the secrets behind this extraordinary lifespan, and it appears to be a complex interplay of environmental, physiological, and molecular factors. Living in an extreme, cold environment and having a remarkably slow metabolism likely plays a significant role, reducing the overall wear and tear on its body over time. Its incredibly late sexual maturation also contributes, as it delays the energetic costs associated with reproduction.

At a more fundamental level, the animal exhibits remarkable biological characteristics that help it resist the effects of aging. Its genetic makeup includes duplications of genes responsible for repairing DNA damage, and variations in a crucial protein called p53, which acts as a tumor suppressor. These features suggest an enhanced ability to maintain the integrity of its genetic material. Furthermore, it possesses robust systems for maintaining protein balance (proteostatic resilience), strong antioxidant defenses to combat cellular stress, and specialized immune adaptations. Emerging evidence also points to a resistance to age-related decline in vital functions like vision and heart performance. Recent genomic studies have also highlighted unique changes in proteins that help package DNA, potentially making its genetic material more stable and protected from damage. The expansion of genes involved in iron regulation also suggests a boosted capacity to control oxidative stress, which can damage DNA. These combined adaptations offer a fascinating glimpse into the mechanisms that allow this creature to defy conventional aging processes.
